title: Python
description: Learn Python with crystal-clear daily life examples, simple English, and clean bullet points across 28 step-by-step lessons.

lessons.title: 1. What is Python?
lessons.explanationHtml:
What is Python?

  • Simple Language: Python is a computer language designed to look like normal English.
  • No Translation Delay: Runs line-by-line so you see results immediately.

Real-World Analogy

  • Think of Python like talking to a helpful assistant. Instead of giving complicated code, you give plain instructions like "print this text" or "add these numbers".

Where is it Used?

  • YouTube & Instagram: Used to show videos and photos on your screen.
  • AI & Robots: Used to train smart assistants like ChatGPT.

Practice Exercise

  • Think of one app on your phone that might use Python to process data.
lessons.codeExample:
# Welcome to Python!
print("Python is ready to help you!")

lessons.title: 2. Your First Program (Hello World)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Hello World

  • print(): Tells the computer to display something on the screen.
  • Quotes: Text goes inside double "..." or single '...' quotes.

Real-World Analogy

  • Using print() is like writing a message on a sticky note and handing it to a friend.

️ Important Rule

  • Incorrect: Print("Hello") (Capital P will crash!).
  • Correct: Always use lowercase print("Hello").

Practice Exercise

  • Print your name and your favorite food on the screen.
lessons.codeExample:
print("Hello, World!")
print("My name is Student!")

lessons.title: 3. Python Syntax & Indentation
lessons.explanationHtml:
How Python Code is Formatted

  • No Curly Braces: Python uses 4 spaces (indentation) to group code together.
  • Line by Line: Each line is a new instruction. No semicolons needed!

Real-World Analogy

  • Indentation is like writing bullet points in a notebook under a main topic heading.

Common Pitfalls & Fixes

  • Incorrect: Forgetting to indent inside a block causes an IndentationError.

lessons.title: 4. Python Comments
lessons.explanationHtml:
What are Comments?

  • Notes for Humans: Computer ignores these lines completely.
  • Starts with a hash symbol #.

Real-World Analogy

  • Comments are like sticky note reminders written in the margins of a textbook.
lessons.codeExample:
# This is a comment. Computer will ignore this line.
print("This line will run!") # Inline comment
lessons.tryItDefault:
# Add your comment here
print("Comments help explain code!")

lessons.title: 5. Variables (Labeled Storage Boxes)
lessons.explanationHtml:
What is a Variable?

  • Storage Box: A named container that holds information in memory.
  • You give it a name, an equals sign =, and put a value inside.

Real-World Analogy

  • Think of a shoe box labeled "Winter Shoes". The label is the variable name, and the shoes inside are the value.
lessons.codeExample:
student_name = "Alex"
age = 18
print(student_name)
print(age)

lessons.title: 6. Variable Naming Rules
lessons.explanationHtml:
Rules for Variable Names

  • Must start with a letter or an underscore _.
  • Cannot start with a number (e.g. 1st_place is invalid).
  • Use snake_case (lowercase words separated by underscores).

Real-World Analogy

  • Labeling boxes clearly: user_home_address is easy to read, while a1 is confusing.
lessons.codeExample:
# Good variable names
user_age = 25
total_price = 99.99

# Bad variable names (Avoid these!)
# 1user = "John" -> Error!
# user-name = "John" -> Error!

lessons.title: 7. Python Data Types Overview
lessons.explanationHtml:
Basic Data Types

  • Text (str): Words wrapped in quotes e.g. "Hello".
  • Whole Number (int): Numbers without decimals e.g. 25.
  • Decimal Number (float): Numbers with decimals e.g. 19.99.
  • True/False (bool): Yes or No values (True / False).

Real-World Analogy

  • Text = Your name ("Rahul"), Integer = Your age (20), Float = Price of milk ($3.50), Bool = Light switch (ON/OFF).
lessons.codeExample:
name = "Rahul"
age = 20
price = 3.50
is_student = True

print(type(name))
print(type(age))

lessons.title: 8. Numbers (Integers & Floats)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Integers vs Floats

  • int: Positives, negatives, zero (e.g. -5, 0, 100).
  • float: Numbers with fractional decimal points (e.g. 2.5, -0.01).

Real-World Analogy

  • Integers = Counting people in a room (You can't have 2.5 people!). Floats = Measuring weight (e.g. 65.4 kg).
lessons.codeExample:
people = 5      # int
weight = 65.4   # float

print(people + 2)
print(weight * 2)

lessons.title: 9. Type Casting (Converting Types)
lessons.explanationHtml:
What is Type Casting?

  • Changing data from one type to another.
  • int("10") converts text "10" into number 10.
  • str(25) converts number 25 into text "25".

Real-World Analogy

  • Converting written text on a price tag ("$50") into a number so you can calculate your change at the counter.
lessons.codeExample:
price_text = "50"
price_number = int(price_text)

total = price_number + 10
print(total) # 60

lessons.title: 10. Strings (Working with Text)
lessons.explanationHtml:
What is a String?

  • Sequence of text characters inside quotes.
  • You can combine strings using the + operator (Concatenation).

Real-World Analogy

  • Stitching your First Name and Last Name together to create your Full Name.
lessons.codeExample:
first_name = "Rahul"
last_name = "Sharma"

full_name = first_name + " " + last_name
print(full_name)

lessons.title: 11. String Methods (Upper, Lower, Replace)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Useful String Tools

  • .upper(): Converts all letters to CAPITAL.
  • .lower(): Converts all letters to small.
  • .replace("old", "new"): Swaps words in text.
  • len(text): Counts how many letters are in the text.

Real-World Analogy

  • Auto-correct capitalization on a form submission.
lessons.codeExample:
msg = "hello world"
print(msg.upper())       # "HELLO WORLD"
print(msg.replace("world", "python")) # "hello python"
print(len(msg))         # 11

lessons.title: 12. F-Strings (Smart Text Formatting)
lessons.explanationHtml:
What is an F-String?

  • Easiest way to insert variables straight into text.
  • Put an f in front of quotes: f"Hello {variable}".

Real-World Analogy

  • Printing an ATM receipt: "Hello [Name], your balance is $[Balance]".
lessons.codeExample:
name = "Amit"
balance = 500

receipt = f"Hello {name}, your balance is \${balance}."
print(receipt)

lessons.title: 13. Booleans (True / False Switches)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Yes or No Answers

  • Booleans hold only two values: True or False.
  • Notice the capital T and F!

Real-World Analogy

  • Is the door locked? True or False. Is the battery full? True or False.
lessons.codeExample:
is_online = True
is_admin = False

print(10 > 5) # Evaluates to True
print(3 == 7) # Evaluates to False

lessons.title: 14. Math Operators (+, -, *, /)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Calculator Math

  • + (Add), - (Subtract), * (Multiply), / (Divide)
  • % (Remainder / Modulo): Gives what's left over after division.

Real-World Analogy

  • Using modulo % 2 to see if a number of chocolates can be divided evenly between 2 friends.
lessons.codeExample:
print(10 + 5) # 15
print(10 * 3) # 30
print(10 / 2) # 5.0
print(10 % 3) # 1 (Remainder)

lessons.title: 15. Comparing Values (==, !=, >, <)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Comparing Two Things

  • == (Is Equal to?)
  • != (Is NOT Equal to?)
  • > (Greater than), < (Less than)

Real-World Analogy

  • Checking if your exam score (85) is greater than the passing mark (50).
lessons.codeExample:
my_score = 85
pass_mark = 50

print(my_score >= pass_mark) # True
print(my_score == 100)       # False

lessons.title: 16. Logical Operators (and, or, not)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Combining Decisions

  • and: BOTH conditions must be True.
  • or: AT LEAST ONE condition must be True.
  • not: Flips True to False, or False to True.

Real-World Analogy

  • To enter a movie theater, you need a Ticket and ID.
lessons.codeExample:
has_ticket = True
has_id = True

can_enter = has_ticket and has_id
print(can_enter) # True

lessons.title: 17. Lists (Shopping Lists)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Storing Multiple Items

  • A list holds items in order inside square brackets [...].
  • Items can be numbers, text, or booleans.

Real-World Analogy

  • A grocery shopping list: ["Milk", "Eggs", "Bread"].
lessons.codeExample:
shopping_list = ["Milk", "Eggs", "Bread"]
print(shopping_list[0]) # First item: "Milk"
print(len(shopping_list)) # Total items: 3

lessons.title: 18. List Operations (Add & Remove)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Modifying Lists

  • .append("item"): Adds new item to the end.
  • .remove("item"): Removes specific item.
  • .pop(): Removes the last item.

Real-World Analogy

  • Adding a new song to your playlist or deleting a song you don't like.
lessons.codeExample:
playlist = ["Song 1", "Song 2"]
playlist.append("Song 3")
print(playlist)

playlist.remove("Song 1")
print(playlist)

lessons.title: 19. Tuples (Locked Lists)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Fixed Lists

  • Tuples store items inside round brackets (...).
  • Once created, you CANNOT change or edit items.

Real-World Analogy

  • Your Date of Birth (Day, Month, Year) - it will never change for the rest of your life!
lessons.codeExample:
dob = (15, "August", 1947)
print(dob[0])
# dob[0] = 16 # ERROR! Cannot change tuple items!

lessons.title: 20. Dictionaries (Contact Cards)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Key and Value Pairs

  • Stores items in { "key": "value" } format inside curly braces.
  • Used to store details about a single person or item.

Real-World Analogy

  • A phone contact card: Name = "Ankit", Phone = "9876543210".
lessons.codeExample:
contact = {
  "name": "Ankit",
  "phone": "9876543210",
  "city": "Delhi"
}

print(contact["name"])
print(contact["city"])

lessons.title: 21. If...Else (Traffic Signals)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Making Decisions in Code

  • if: Runs if condition is True.
  • elif: Checks next condition if first was False.
  • else: Runs if no conditions were True.

Real-World Analogy

  • Traffic Signal: IF light is Green -> Go. ELIF light is Yellow -> Slow down. ELSE -> Stop.

lessons.title: 22. While Loops (Repetition)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Repeating Code

  • Keeps running code as long as a condition remains True.
  • Be careful: Always update counter so loop eventually stops!

Real-World Analogy

  • Brushing teeth until 2 minutes are up.
lessons.codeExample:
count = 1
while count <= 3:
    print(f"Step \${count}")
    count += 1

lessons.title: 23. For Loops (Going Through Lists)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Step Through Each Item

  • Loops through every item in a list or sequence one by one.

Real-World Analogy

  • A teacher calling roll call out loud for every student in a classroom list.

lessons.title: 24. Functions (Recipe Machines)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Reusable Commands

  • Define a function using def function_name():.
  • Write code once, call it whenever you need!

Real-World Analogy

  • A Juicer Machine: You input fruits (ingredients), press button, and it returns fresh juice!
lessons.codeExample:
def make_juice(fruit):
    return f"Here is your fresh \${fruit} juice!"

glass = make_juice("Mango")
print(glass)

lessons.title: 25. Try...Except (Safety Nets)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Preventing Crashes

  • Put risky code inside try: block.
  • If an error occurs, except: catches it without crashing app!

Real-World Analogy

  • Wearing a seatbelt in a car. It's a safety net in case of unexpected bumps.

lessons.title: 26. File Handling (Reading & Writing Text)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Saving Data to Files

  • open("file.txt", "w"): Write new file.
  • open("file.txt", "r"): Read existing file.

Real-World Analogy

  • Saving your notes into a notepad text document on your laptop.
lessons.codeExample:
# Write to file
with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Python is awesome!")

print("File saved successfully!")
lessons.tryItDefault: print("File operations let you store notes on disk!")

lessons.title: 27. Classes & Objects (Blueprints)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Blueprints vs Real Objects

  • Class: Architectural blueprint (e.g. Car Design).
  • Object: The actual car built from the blueprint.

Real-World Analogy

  • A cookie cutter is the Class. Every cookie stamped out is an Object!

lessons.title: 28. Capstone Project: Simple Calculator CLI
lessons.explanationHtml:
Put It All Together!

  • You will combine user inputs, math operators, functions, and loops!

Real-World Project

  • Build a functional command-line calculator that adds, subtracts, and multiplies numbers.
lessons.codeExample:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

num1 = 10
num2 = 20
result = add(num1, num2)
print(f"Result: \${num1} + \${num2} = \${result}")
lessons.tryItDefault: print("Congratulations on reaching the Python Capstone!")
